notes.meaning: After King Amaziah died, the people of Judah agreed together to put his young son on the throne. Uzziah was only sixteen. In 2 Kings he is also called Azariah.

Eloth, also called Elath, was a port town on the Red Sea. Uzziah made it strong again and won it back for Judah early in his reign. The writer puts this first, before the usual facts about his reign, because it was what he was known for. The port mattered for trade with lands to the east.
These are the basic facts of his reign. He started at sixteen and ruled for fifty-two years, a long time. His mother, Jecoliah, was from Jerusalem.

Uzziah kept up the true worship of God, as his father had. Matthew Henry says he was not especially zealous, yet in one way he was better than his father. There is no sign he ever worshiped idols, even later when he grew proud.

Zechariah was a wise and godly adviser, and maybe the king's teacher. He helped Uzziah learn to honor God. He was not the Zechariah killed under King Joash. While Uzziah kept seeking God, God made him do well. Success is God's gift, and God never turns away from those who truly seek him. Matthew Henry adds a warning: it is sad to seek God only while a good adviser is near.

Uzziah beat the Philistines, Israel's old enemies. He broke down the walls of their cities and built his own towns among them to keep them under control. The writer says plainly that God helped him. He also beat Arab peoples who had once raided Judah.

The Ammonites paid Uzziah tribute, which is regular payment showing they were under him. His name became known as far as the edge of Egypt, because his rule reached that far. Matthew Henry says it was a good name, the kind that truly honors a person.

Uzziah built strong towers at the weak spots in Jerusalem's walls. Some of the wall had been broken down in his father's time. Matthew Henry says the city's best defense was still his faithfulness to God.

Out in the wild country, Uzziah built towers to guard his herds and shepherds from raiders. He dug wells so the animals had water. He loved farming and kept farmers and vine growers busy. The commentators praise this as a good thing in a king. He did not live for war or pleasure, and his example urged his people to work hard on the land.

Uzziah had a large army, carefully counted and split into groups. The groups were based on family clans, each led by a brave head of a family. Officials who were skilled with records kept the lists. It was a strong force ready to defend the king.

Uzziah gave the whole army its gear, both for defense and for attack. That way weapons were ready for anyone who had to fight. Matthew Henry notes that swords are not listed, likely because each man already had his own.

Clever men built machines for Jerusalem's towers that could shoot arrows and throw big stones. Adam Clarke thinks this may be the first such war machine on record. The key point comes at the end: Uzziah was "helped tremendously". God was the reason he became strong.

Here is the turning point. Success made Uzziah proud, and pride led to his fall. Instead of thanking God for all his help, he forgot God and lifted himself up. He went into the holy place, where only priests could go, to burn incense himself. Earlier kings had sinned by leaving God's temple for idols. Uzziah sinned the other way, by pushing too far into it.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars have thought Uzziah only wanted to bring back a priestly role that kings like David and Solomon had. Keil & Delitzsch answer that those kings led worship but never did the duties kept for priests.

notes.meaning: Azariah the high priest followed the king in with eighty other priests. They are called brave because it took courage to face such a powerful king.

The priests did not grab the king. They stood against him with words. God's law gave the burning of incense only to Aaron's family, the priests set apart for it. Their warning that he would get no honor from God was gently put, but it meant God would punish him. The Geneva Notes say that even if his zeal looked good, it was wrong because it did not follow God's word. Matthew Henry adds that the jobs of king and priest were meant to come together only in the Messiah. He also says our prayers reach God through Jesus, our great High Priest.

Instead of listening, Uzziah got angry and held on to the censer, the pan for burning incense. Right then, beside the altar, leprosy broke out on his forehead. It was a serious skin disease that made a person unclean. Wesley notes that it showed on his face, so he could not hide his shame, and that it clearly came from God. Matthew Henry says that if he had admitted his error and left, all would have been well.

When the priests saw the leprosy, they hurried him out, and Uzziah himself rushed to leave. He knew the Lord had struck him. Matthew Henry sees some real fear of God in this. The king argued with the priests, but he would not argue with his Maker.

Uzziah stayed a leper until he died. As God's law required, he lived in a separate house, shut out from the temple and from public life. His son Jotham ruled for him. The commentators say the punishment matched the sin like a face in a mirror. He pushed into a place only priests could enter, so he lost even the temple courts. He reached for a priest's honor and lost his own royal honor. Matthew Henry hopes Uzziah used those quiet years to repent and get ready to meet God.
The prophet Isaiah wrote a fuller record of Uzziah's reign. Adam Clarke notes that this record is now lost. In the book of Isaiah, Uzziah is only mentioned briefly.

Uzziah was buried in a field that belonged to the kings, near their tombs but not inside them. People thought a leper's body would make the royal graves unclean. So the shame of his sin followed him even in death and darkened all his earlier glory.
